newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Growing trade gap dims Vietnam's economic glory.
newsitem.headline: Growing trade gap dims Vietnam's economic glory.

text.p: Vietnam said Monday its trade deficit soared by more than 80 percent to a record $4.0 billion in 1996 as its burgeoning economy pulled in imports faster than it could produce goods for sale abroad.

The government's General Statistics Office estimated the volume of exports for the whole year at $7.1 billion and imports at $11.1 billion, creating a trade gap nearly 82 percent higher than 1995's $2.2 billion.

Analysts said the ballooning trade deficit took the gloss off another year of stellar economic growth and laid bare the shortcomings of the communist government's 10-year-old drive for reform along market lines.

"Our road to development has been paved with glory, but our country still has to overcome many difficulties, trials and challenges," Minister of Planning and Investment Tran Xuan Gia wrote in the latest weekly Vietnam Investment Review.

Gia said gross domestic product had grown by 9.5 percent in 1996 -- one of the fastest rates in the world -- while industrial production had increased by 14 percent and inflation had been brought under control at just 4.5 percent.
However, he said, the government was faced with an array of other problems in addition to the trade deficit, which Monday's figures showed was equivalent to about 18 percent of annual GDP.
"If this is not solved, it will lead to the collapse of our trade and payment balance in coming years," Gia said.

Until recently, the government had argued that it was normal for economies in transition to record trade deficits as they import capital goods for the development of industry, which would in the long run generate goods for export.

However, many such imports go to low-productivity, loss-making state enterprises and consumer goods now account for a growing share of the country's imports because years of pent-up demand has been unleashed by an explosion in disposable income.
